description:
I am a passionate space and technology enthusiast with a background in engineering and a very creative approach to problem solving. I enjoy turning complex data into clear solutions and I am motivated to build an innovative and meaningful app during this challenge. 

My project is focused on turning NASA`s open data into a clear, creative and technically solid solution and combine scientific mindset with creativity to deliver a project well documented and easy to understand.
summary:
Tombaugh Scope is a browser-based observatory for hunting a hypothetical Planet X in SPHEREx data, using the same idea Clyde Tombaugh used to discover Pluto: blinking images of the same sky taken at different times, so that anything that moves stands out against the fixed stars.

Users can load real SPHEREx FITS images, blink them, subtract one epoch from another, mask cosmic rays and overlay Gaia and WISE catalogues to rule out known stars. Candidates are checked against expected motion, and an analysis workspace gathers the results into a report. A 3D Solar System with real planetary positions and an immersive flight mode shows where such an object could lie and why it is so hard to find.

The tool needs no installation and runs in any browser, so students, citizen scientists and researchers can inspect the same data and understand how a discovery is made. It does not claim a detection. It makes the search method visible, reproducible and accessible, which is why it matters for SPHEREx’s all-sky survey and for the search for the Solar System’s outer planets.
details:
What it does. Tombaugh Scope is a browserbased observatory for searching for a hypothetical Planet X in SPHEREx data. It uses the method Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto: blinking images of the same sky taken at different times, so that anything that moves stands out against the fixed stars. Users can load real SPHEREx FITS images, blink them between epochs and bands, subtract one image from another, mask cosmic rays, and overlay Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalogues (live from VizieR) to rule out known stars. A blind detection step flags moving objects and variables, which can be checked frame by frame. An analysis workspace scores candidates and produces a report. A sky map, a 3D Solar System and an immersive flight mode show where such an object could lie and why it is so hard to find.

Benefits and impact. The tool needs no installation and runs in any browser, in five languages, so students, citizen scientists and researchers can inspect the same data and see how a discovery is made. It does not claim a detection. Its aim is to make the search method visible, reproducible and accessible for SPHEREx’s all-sky survey and for the search for outer Solar System planets.

Data and honesty. Real: SPHEREx FITS files that the user loads, the SPHEREx all-sky image (reduced resolution), HYG star positions, and Gaia/WISE overlays. Computed: planet positions from orbital elements for the chosen date. Simulated or illustrative: the default Field · Blink field (a physical model, labelled SIM), the Planet X orbit, the SPX-01…03 markers and the demo analysis scene. The detection was tested on the asteroid Pallas, recovered within about 1.1 pixels (about 7″) of JPL Horizons; the settings were tuned on Pallas, so this is not yet an independent test.

Tools. A single HTML file built with JavaScript, Canvas and WebGL, with browser storage so loaded data persists. Testing used headless Chromium. Data sources: NASA SPHEREx via IRSA, Gaia DR3 and AllWISE via VizieR, the HYG catalogue, JPL Horizons for validation, and planet textures from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0). The app was developed with the help of an AI assistant (Claude).

The code, user-interface design, translations and the text of the presentation were developed with the help of an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic), directed, reviewed and tested by the author. The project contains no SI-generated images, video or audio.

Creativity and factors considered. I turned a historic discovery method into an interactive, honest tool, and labeled clearly what is real, computed or simulated. I also considered accessibility, performance in the browser, and the limits of the data.
